content.text: How does a power station produce electricity? The answer is generators—devices that convert kinetic energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. Whether powered by steam, wind, or water, generators are the source of almost all the electricity we use.

A generator is the reverse of a motor. It converts kinetic energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field. The changing magnetic flux through the coil induces a voltage (electromagnetic induction).
A generator converts kinetic (rotational) energy into electrical energy:
A coil rotates in a magnetic field
Magnetic flux through the coil changes continuously
This induces a voltage across the coil
If connected to a circuit, current flows
This is the reverse of a motor—instead of current causing rotation, rotation causes current.

When describing the voltage output of an AC generator, remember that the voltage is maximum when the coil is horizontal (cutting field lines fastest) and zero when the coil is vertical (moving parallel to field lines). This is the opposite of what many students expect.
The induced voltage is greater with:

|--------|--------|
| Faster rotation | Higher frequency AND amplitude |
| Stronger magnets | Higher amplitude |
| More turns on coil | Higher amplitude |
| Larger coil area | Higher amplitude |
UK mains: 50 Hz requires 3000 rpm (for simple generator)

Explain the difference between a DC generator and an AC generator.
Both use electromagnetic induction in a rotating coil. The difference is in how they connect to the external circuit:
AC generator: uses slip rings, output alternates direction
DC generator: uses split-ring commutator, output is always in one direction (though it still varies in magnitude)

— AC generators use slip rings. Only DC generators/motors need commutators.
"Generator and motor are completely different devices"
— They're essentially the same device. A motor converts electrical to kinetic; a generator does the opposite.

Rotating coil in magnetic field induces voltage

A coil rotates in a magnetic field. As it turns, the magnetic flux through the coil continuously changes, inducing a voltage. When the coil sides move upward they cut field lines in one direction (positive voltage); when they move downward they cut in the opposite direction (negative voltage). This produces a sinusoidal alternating output.

When the coil is vertical, its sides are moving perpendicular to the field lines, cutting through them at the maximum rate. The rate of change of flux is greatest at this position, so the induced voltage is at its peak.
— Frequency equals the number of complete rotations per second. (calculation)

Slip rings are two complete metal rings, each connected to one end of the coil; they allow continuous contact and produce AC output. A commutator is a single ring split into two halves; it reverses the external connection every half turn, converting the AC generated in the coil into pulsating DC output.

All generators on the grid must be synchronised. If one generator produced a different frequency, its AC cycle would be out of phase with the rest, causing destructive interference, equipment damage, and power instability.
